title: Imaging atomic-scale surface structure and superconducting gap of the misfit layered compound (SnS)1.17NbS2
authors: Dongming Zhao, Shamarita Deb, Lichen Ji, Souvik Das, Paul Simon, Raúl Cardoso-Gil, Steffen Wirth, Walter Schnelle, Sushmita Chandra, Jian-Feng Ge, Claudia Felser
abstract: Superlattices of van der Waals-coupled two-dimensional materials offer a platform for engineering electronic band structure and fostering emergent quantum states. Misfit layered compounds provide naturally assembled superlattices, in which crystallographically distinct two-dimensional subsystems coexist within a single bulk crystal. Therein, the presence of both commensurate and incommensurate lattice directions introduces structural modulation, which might alter real-space electronic orders such as superconductivity. Here, we investigate the atomic-scale surface structure and local superconductivity of the misfit layered compound (SnS)1.17NbS2 using structural characterization, electrical transport, and low-temperature scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM). While X-ray diffraction and cross-sectional scanning transmission electron microscopy confirm the bulk misfit structure, STM resolves large SnS- and NbS2-terminated terraces, where the surface atomic registry differs from the bulk misfit structure. Furthermore, tunnelling spectroscopy at 2 K reveals nearly identical superconducting gaps on both terminations, and the spatial variation of the gap shows no visible modulation that corresponds to the misfit lattice. These results establish an atomic-scale picture of the surface structure and superconducting states of this naturally assembled misfit heterostructure.
summary: This work characterizes the atomic-scale structure and superconductivity of the misfit layered compound (SnS)1.17NbS2. Using STM and STS, the authors found that while the surface structure differs from the bulk, the superconducting gap remains remarkably uniform across both SnS and NbS2 terminations. This establishes an atomic-scale picture of the superconducting state in this naturally assembled heterostructure.
main_problem: The study investigates the atomic-scale surface structure and local superconducting gap of the misfit layered compound (SnS)1.17NbS2, specifically addressing how surface termination affects electronic properties.
main_result: The superconducting gap was found to be nearly identical on both SnS and NbS2 terminations, suggesting coherence across the layers, despite the surface structure differing from the bulk misfit arrangement.
method: The research employed a combination of structural characterization (XRD, STEM) and local electronic measurements using low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS).
model_or_system: The physical system is the misfit layered compound (SnS)1.17NbS2, which naturally forms an alternating superlattice of SnS and NbS2 sublayers. The investigation focuses on the electronic states at the surface terminations.
key_observables: Superconducting gap ($\Delta$), surface atomic registry, and electrical resistivity ($ho(T)$).
important_parameters: Superconducting gap size ($\approx 0.33 	ext{ meV}$), temperature ($2 	ext{ K}$), and the misfit lattice periodicity.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the surface structure relaxation on the SnS termination is due to the bulk configuration being energetically unfavorable. The gap size comparison relies on fitting spectra using the Dynes formula.
figures_summary: Figures show structural confirmation via XRD/STEM, STM images revealing distinct SnS and NbS2 terminations, and STS spectra confirming a uniform superconducting gap across both surfaces.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first confirming the bulk misfit structure using XRD and STEM. It then uses STM to resolve the distinct surface terminations (SnS vs. NbS2). Finally, STS measurements are performed to map the superconducting gap on these surfaces, comparing the results to the bulk structural context.
why_interesting: While focused on superconductivity, the use of STM to resolve atomic-scale structural differences and map local electronic order parameters provides a model for studying how structural mismatch or surface reconstruction can influence emergent quantum states in heterostructures.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Structural characterization of (SnS)1.17NbS2. (a) Crystal structure of (SnS)1.17NbS2 along the b axis. Sn, Nb, and S atoms are represented in green, magenta, and yellow, respectively. (b) X-ray diffraction pattern of the (SnS)1.17NbS2 single crystal. Inset: a photograph of the as-grown single crystal. (c) Cross-sectional STEM image along the [010] axis showing the alternating stacking of SnS and NbS2 layers. The structural model is overlaid for comparison.

Fig. 2 Surface structure of (SnS)1.17NbS2. (a) Large-area STM topography showing adjacent SnS- and NbS2-terminated regions (Vbias = 100 mV, Iset = 30 pA). The boxes indicate the regions enlarged in (c) and (d). The lower panel shows the height profile extracted along the orange line in the topographic image. (b) Top-view structural model illustrating the relative registry of the SnS and NbS2 layers at the surface. The blue square marks the smallest square structural unit resolved experimentally on the SnS termination, corresponding to a characteristic Sn–S spacing of approximately 0.33 nm. (c) Atomic-resolution STM topography of the SnS termination (Vbias = −100 mV, Iset = 50 pA). (d)...

Fig. 3 Superconductivity of (SnS)1.17NbS2. (a) Temperature dependence of the resistivity near the superconducting transition with an onset of 2.7 K. Inset: resistivity over the full measured temperature range. Tunnelling spectra measured at 2.0 K (~ 0.75 Tc) on (b) the SnS and (c) the NbS2 terminations, respectively. Solid curves show fitting by the Dynes formula. The fitted superconducting gap is Δ = 0.33 meV for both terminations. Set point: Vbias = -3 mV, Iset =100 pA, Vmod = 0.06 mV.

Fig. 4 Spatial variation of the superconducting gap on the SnS termination. (a) STM topography of the 4 × 4 nm2 spectroscopic mapping area. (b) Spatial distribution of the superconducting gap Δ obtained from Dynes fits to the local tunnelling spectra.
